$comment: Mutants for tools/verify-mutation.mjs. Each entry is a defect a person
could plausibly write, paired with the test(s) that must catch it.
`find` and `replace` are arrays of source lines, joined with \n. Whitespace
is significant — the anchor must match the file exactly, and must match it
Adding a mutant is how you assert that a piece of behaviour is genuinely
covered. Removing one because it fails is how the gate stops meaning

mutants.why: A live region only announces when its content CHANGES. Setting textContent directly makes a repeated message silent — the single most common way this class of service is subtly broken.
expectFailing: is OBSERVED to change when the same message is announced twice
empties the region synchronously, before the text arrives

mutants.why: Creating the regions in the constructor rather than on first use. Costs every app that never announces, and on the server produces a node the client then has to reconcile — a hydration mismatch.
expectFailing: creates nothing until something is announced
ignores an empty or whitespace-only message, and stays inert doing it

mutants.why: Teardown that empties the regions but never removes them. Each destroyed injector leaves two nodes in the accessibility tree; nothing visibly breaks until a screen reader is reading a page with dozens of them.
expectFailing: removes its regions when the injector is destroyed

mutants.why: Announcing on the server. There is no DOM to announce into, and the attempt either throws during SSR or emits markup the client never expects.
expectFailing: touches no DOM

mutants.why: clear() that empties the regions but leaves the pending timeout armed. The message lands a task later, so a view torn down mid-announcement still gets read out, describing something that is gone.
expectFailing: does not announce a message that clear() overtook

mutants.why: One region with a flipped aria-live attribute instead of two. Politeness is read when a region is first encountered, so the flip is unreliable and an assertive message can be delivered politely — or not at all.
expectFailing: routes politeness to separate regions

mutants.why: uniqueId returning a constant suffix. Duplicate ids silently break every aria-labelledby and aria-describedby that points at one — the label resolves to whichever element the browser found first.
expectFailing: never returns the same id twice

mutants.why: The `type` default set to submit — or simply omitted, which means the same thing inside a form. A "Cancel" button then submits the form, and nothing reveals it until the button is placed in a form, possibly months later.
expectFailing: renders type="button"
does not submit the form it sits in — which is why the default exists

mutants.why: The variant class without the base class. Every layout declaration lives on .tk-button and the variant only re-points tokens, so the button loses its size, padding, focus ring and hit target while still looking like it has a variant applied.
expectFailing: carries the base class as well as the variant

mutants.why: The class string hard-coded instead of computed from the input. The default appearance still renders correctly, so every test that only checks the default passes — and the input silently does nothing.
expectFailing: swaps the variant class when the input changes, leaving no stale one

mutants.why: A generated id always winning. Any aria-labelledby or popovertarget a consumer wrote against their own id points at nothing — and IDREFs fail silently, so the control renders looking correct and unlabelled.
find: protected readonly resolvedId = computed(() => this.id() ?? this.generatedId);
expectFailing: lets an explicit id win

mutants.why: Never assigning the indeterminate DOM property. It has no HTML attribute, so a template binding writes something the platform ignores: the checkbox renders as plain unchecked while every attribute-reading test agrees with itself.
expectFailing: sets the DOM property, which has no HTML attribute

mutants.why: Toggling the model instead of reading what the platform decided. It agrees with the element until one change event is missed or replayed, after which the box and the model disagree permanently and nothing says so.
expectFailing: takes the new state FROM the element, not from flipping the model

mutants.why: effectivelyDisabled reading only the author's input. Reactive Forms' control.disable() then does nothing visible, and a disabled form stays interactive. (The catching test is in the checkbox's compat integration suite, because the two channels only disagree when a form is attached.)
expectFailing: disables the control when the form disables it

mutants.why: Rendering name="" instead of omitting the attribute. A submitted field with an empty name is not the same as a field that does not submit.
find: protected readonly nameAttr = computed(() => this.name() || null);
expectFailing: is absent rather than empty when unset

mutants.why: The classic hand-rolled-adapter bug: reporting every model change to the form, including the adapter's own writeValue. A signal effect is SCHEDULED, not inline, so the obvious boolean flag is already cleared when it runs. The form goes dirty the moment it is populated, and loops if anything reacts to valueChanges.
find: // The echo of our own writeValue: swallowed exactly once.
expectFailing: does not mark the form dirty when the FORM set the value

mutants.why: Remembering the form's value permanently instead of consuming the guard once. Looks correct until the user sets the same value the form last wrote, at which point a real edit silently disappears.
expectFailing: still reports a user edit that happens to match an earlier form write

mutants.why: setDisabledState writing nothing. Reactive Forms believes the control is disabled and the user can still click it.
expectFailing: routes a form disable to disabledByForm, not to the author input

$removed.why: NOT removed to make the gate pass. The gate showed the code it targeted was dead: Angular's setUpControl calls writeValue synchronously during the directive's first ngOnChanges, before any effect flushes, so the pending-value guard already covers the first run. The skip was deleted; a mutant describing code that no longer exists describes nothing.
